items.title: 67247_J.C. Higginbotham oral history interview
items.q: But Jay Jay Johnson, that was nothing but just technician, everything is going-going-going-going, and you don't know what's happening. I didn't; maybe they did.

ctx.x: He had two trombones. He had Claude Jones and Benny Morton... He let Claude go and Benny and I worked together.

Oh, that's it, they did work together. I saw the picture of them too in the book and I was wondering if that was - ... You were also telling us yesterday a little bit of how you reacted to trombone players such as Jay Jay Johnson, Benny Green, and their style. You said that their style was a little too technical to suit you?
No, I didn't say they - I said Jay Jay.

items.title: 67247_J.C. Higginbotham oral history interview
items.q: I don't know very much technically about the trombone playing but he tells me that before J. J. Johnson... there was a style of playing

ctx.x: I think he's made a significant contribution in the way he has played. I talked to Joe,

I don't know very much technically about the trombone playing but he tells me that before J. J. Johnson, that is, youknow during my father's time, there was a style of playing where they used a lot of lip slurs and now it's mostly through counting and staccato with the trombone where it used to be slurring ... And I think as a representative of the lip ... style, he was the best.

I've listened to some old recordings and I've listened tremendously to Kid Ory, Jack Teagarden was about like was overrated. That's without saying that Paul Whiteman, the King of Swing or something is usually a white representative that they put on top of the instrument and I don't agree with it. I think he was absolutely the best and I think he ought to be given credit for me that.
